It has been said that "la" (لَا) is a redundant particle (ṣila), and its occurrence at the beginning of the surah is permissible because the Qur'an is connected, one part to another, so it has the status of a single speech. The meaning of the sentence is: "I swear by the Day of Resurrection." This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr and Abu 'Ubayda, and similar to it is the words of the poet:

*I remembered Layla, and passion overcame me,*
*so that the core of my heart nearly was cut to pieces.*

Abu al-Layth al-Samarqandi related: The exegetes agreed that the meaning of "la uqsimu" is "uqsimu" (I swear). They differed over the explanation of "la." Others said: "la" is a rejection of their statement, since they denied the Resurrection, so He says: "The matter is not as you claim." I say: This is the view of al-Farra'. Al-Farra' said: Many grammarians say that "la" is a redundant particle, but it is not permissible to begin with a negation and then make it redundant, because if that were so, a statement containing a negation could not be distinguished from a statement without negation. This is like their saying: "No, by God, I will not do it," where "la" is a rejection of a statement that has already passed. It is like your saying: "No, by God, the Resurrection is indeed true," as if you were denying a people who rejected it. Someone other than al-Farra' recited for Imru' al-Qays:

*No, by your father, daughter of al-'Amiri,*
*the people shall not claim that I flee.*

Ghuwayya ibn Sulma said:

*Umama called out, carrying [her load] away, to grieve me;*
*no, by you, I do not care.*

Its benefit is the emphasis of the oath in the refutation. Al-Farra' said: Whoever does not know this aspect recites "la-uqsimu" without an alif, as if it were the lam of emphasis (lam al-ta'kid) that entered upon "uqsimu." This is correct, because the Arabs say "la-uqsimu billah." This is the reading of al-Hasan, Ibn Kathir, al-Zuhri and Ibn Humruz. ﴿by the Day of Resurrection﴾, meaning by a day on which people will stand before their Lord. It is permissible for God, Mighty and Majestic, to swear by whatever He wishes.

(﴿And I swear by the self-reproaching soul﴾) There is no disagreement among the readers about this: He, glory be to Him, swore by the Day of Resurrection to magnify its matter [and He did not swear by the soul [[The addition is from the tafsir of Ibn 'Atiyya and others.]]]. According to the reading of Ibn Kathir, He swore by the first and did not swear by the second. It has been said: "And I swear by the self-reproaching soul" is another refutation and the beginning of an oath by the self-reproaching soul. Al-Tha'labi said: The correct view is that He swore by both of them together. The meaning of "by the self-reproaching soul" is by the soul of the believer, who, whenever you see him, reproaches himself, saying: "What did I intend by such-and-such?" You will see him only rebuking his own soul. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Hasan and others. Al-Hasan said: By God, it is the soul of the believer; the believer is seen only reproaching himself: "What did I intend by my speech? What did I intend by my eating? What did I intend by my inner talk?" The wicked does not hold himself to account. Mujahid said: It is the soul that blames itself for what has passed and regrets it; it blames itself for evil, asking why it did it, and for good, asking why it did not increase it. It has been said: it means the one who blames. It has been said: it blames itself for what it blames others for. According to these views, "al-lawwama" carries the meaning of "al-la'ima" (the one who blames), which is a description of praise, and on this basis the oath by it is appropriate and fine. In some exegesis it is said: Adam, peace be upon him, never ceased to blame himself for his disobedience by which he was expelled from the Garden. It has also been said: "al-lawwama" means "al-malumah al-madhumah" (the one blamed and censured), also from Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Farra' said: There is no soul, whether good or bad, but that it blames itself: the one who does good blames himself that he did not increase his good, and the one who does evil blames himself that he did not refrain from his evil.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Does man think that We will not assemble his bones?﴾ That We will restore them to a new creation after they have become dust. Al-Zajjaj said: I swear by the Day of Resurrection and by the self-reproaching soul: He will certainly assemble the bones for the Resurrection, and this is the response of the oath. Al-Nahhas said: The response of the oath is omitted, meaning "you will certainly be raised," and it is indicated by the words of the Exalted: ﴿Does man think that We will not assemble his bones?﴾, for revival and resurrection. Here "man" means the unbeliever who denies the Resurrection. The verse was revealed concerning 'Adi ibn Rabi'a, who said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Tell me about the Day of Resurrection: when will it be, and what is its matter and state?" The Prophet (ﷺ) informed him of that, and he said: "If I were to witness that day, O Muhammad, I would not believe you, nor would I have faith in it, or would God assemble the bones?!" For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) used to say: "O God, suffice me against the evil neighbours, 'Adi ibn Rabi'a and al-Akhnas ibn Shariq." It has also been said: it was revealed concerning the enemy of God, Abu Jahl, when he denied resurrection after death. He mentioned the bones, and what is meant is the whole of him, because the bones are the frame of the creation. ﴿Yes﴾ is a good pause, then you begin with ﴿able﴾. Sibawayh said: The meaning is "We will assemble them, being able," so "qadirin" is a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the doer hidden in the omitted verb, according to the estimate we have mentioned. It has been said: The meaning is "Nay, We will be able, being able." Al-Farra' said: "Qadirin" is in the accusative by being excluded from "najma'a" (We assemble), meaning: We are able and we are capable of more than that. He also said: Its accusative may be a repetition, meaning "Yes, let them suppose that We are able." It has been said: The hidden element is "kunna" (We were), meaning: We were able at the beginning, and the polytheists had acknowledged this. Ibn Abi 'Abla and Ibn al-Sumayqa' read "Bala qadirun," with the interpretation "We are able."

(﴿to put together even his fingertips﴾) Al-banan in the Arabic language is the fingers, and its singular is "banana." Al-Nabigha said:

*With a delicate, dyed hand, as if its fingers*
*were henna shoots that almost knot from delicacy.* [[The reading of the last half, as in al-Lisan:
"henna upon its branches, which has not knotted."

'Antara said:

*Death is subject to my hand whenever*
*I join her fingers to the Hindi sword.*

By mentioning the fingers he indicated the rest of the limbs. Also, they are the smallest of the bones, so He singled them out for mention for that reason. It has also been said: That is, We are able to return the human being to the form of animals, so how much more in the form in which he was. This is like the words of the Exalted: ﴿And We are not to be outdone, in replacing your likes and bringing you into being in what you do not know﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 60–61]. I say: The first interpretation is more fitting to the context of the verse. And God knows best.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿But man desires to continue in sin ahead of him﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: It means the unbeliever who denies what lies ahead of him, of resurrection and reckoning. Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd also said this, and its evidence is: ﴿He asks, "When is the Day of Resurrection?"﴾, meaning he asks when it will happen, in a manner of denial and rejection. So the Bedouin said:

*Abu Hafs Umar swore by God*
*that no sore and no wound touched them.*
*So forgive him, O God, if he lied.*

Meaning: if he lied to me about what I mentioned. Also from Ibn 'Abbas: he hastens the sin and delays repentance. In some hadith it is said: He says, "I will repent later," and does not repent; so he has broken his word and lied. This is the view of Mujahid, al-Hasan, 'Ikrima, al-Suddi and Sa'id ibn Jubayr: he says, "I will repent, I will repent," until death comes to him in his worst state. It has been said: It means he resolves upon sin forever, even if he lives only a short while. According to these views, the pronoun "hu" (in "li-yafjura amamahu") refers to man. It has been said: The pronoun refers to the Day of Resurrection, and the meaning is: "Man desires to deny the truth before the Day of Resurrection." Fujur is originally deviation from the truth.

(﴿He asks when the Day of Resurrection is﴾) That is, when the Day of Resurrection is.

Al-Farra' said: "Qadirin" is in the accusative by being excluded from "najma'a" (We assemble), meaning: We are able and we are capable of more than that. He also said: Its accusative may be a repetition, meaning "Yes, let them suppose that We are able." It has been said: The hidden element is "kunna" (We were), meaning: We were able at the beginning, and the polytheists had acknowledged this. Ibn Abi 'Abla and Ibn al-Sumayqa' read "Bala qadirun," with the interpretation "We are able."

(﴿to put together even his fingertips﴾) Al-banan in the Arabic language is the fingers, and its singular is "banana." Al-Nabigha said:

*With a delicate, dyed hand, as if its fingers*
*were henna shoots that almost knot from delicacy.* [[The reading of the last half, as in al-Lisan:
"henna upon its branches, which has not knotted."
Al-'anam is a tree with soft, slender branches, to which fingers are compared.]]

'Antara said:

*Death is subject to my hand whenever*
*I join her fingers to the Hindi sword.*

By mentioning the fingers he indicated the rest of the limbs. Also, they are the smallest of the bones, so He singled them out for mention for that reason. Al-Qutaybi and al-Zajjaj said: They claimed that God does not raise the dead and is not able to assemble the bones, so God, Exalted, said: ﴿Yes, We are able to restore the small joints even in their smallness, and to join them together until they become level; and whoever is able to do this is even more able to assemble the large ones.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas and most of the exegetes said: The meaning of ﴿to put together even his fingertips﴾ is that We make the fingers of his hands and feet one thing, like the hoof of a camel, or the hoof of a donkey, or the cloven hoof of a pig, and he cannot do anything with it; but We separated his fingers so that he can take with them whatever he wills. Al-Hasan used to say: He made fingers for you, and you spread them and close them with them; and if God had willed, He would have joined them, and you would not have been able to protect the earth except with your two palms. It has also been said: That is, We are able to return the human being to the form of animals, so how much more in the form in which he was. This is like the words of the Exalted: ﴿And We are not to be outdone, in replacing your likes and bringing you into being in what you do not know﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 60–61]. I say: The first interpretation is more fitting to the context of the verse. And God knows best.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿But man desires to continue in sin ahead of him﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: It means the unbeliever who denies what lies ahead of him, of resurrection and reckoning. Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd also said this, and its evidence is: ﴿He asks, "When is the Day of Resurrection?"﴾, meaning he asks when it will happen, in a manner of denial and rejection. He is not content with the denial he is in, but he persists in sin for what lies ahead of him. Among the things that show that "al-fujur" means denial is what al-Qutaybi and others mentioned: that a Bedouin came to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, and complained to him about the sores of his camels, their chafing and their saddle wounds, and asked him to carry him on other camels, but he did not carry him. *Abu Hafs Umar swore by God*
*that no sore and no wound touched them.*
*So forgive him, O God, if he lied.*

Meaning: if he lied to me about what I mentioned. Also from Ibn 'Abbas: he hastens the sin and delays repentance. In some hadith it is said: He says, "I will repent later," and does not repent; so he has broken his word and lied. This is the view of Mujahid, al-Hasan, 'Ikrima, al-Suddi and Sa'id ibn Jubayr: he says, "I will repent, I will repent," until death comes to him in his worst state. Al-Dahhak said: It is hope; he says, "I will live and enjoy some of the world," and does not remember death. It has been said: It means he resolves upon sin forever, even if he lives only a short while. According to these views, the pronoun "hu" (in "li-yafjura amamahu") refers to man. It has been said: The pronoun refers to the Day of Resurrection, and the meaning is: "Man desires to deny the truth before the Day of Resurrection." Fujur is originally deviation from the truth.

(﴿He asks when the Day of Resurrection is﴾) That is, when the Day of Resurrection is.

Surat al-Qiyamah is Meccan, and it has thirty-nine verses. In the name of God, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful.

In the name of God, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful.

﴿I swear by the Day of Resurrection. And I swear by the self-reproaching soul. Does man think that We will not assemble his bones? Yes, We are able to put together even his fingertips.﴾ ﴿But man desires to continue in sin ahead of him. He asks, "When is the Day of Resurrection?"﴾

It has been said that "la" (لَا) is a redundant particle (ṣila), and its occurrence at the beginning of the surah is permissible because the Qur'an is connected, one part to another, so it has the status of a single speech. For this reason, something may be mentioned in one surah while its response (jawab) comes in another surah, as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿They said, "O you to whom the Reminder has been sent, you are indeed a madman!"﴾ [al-Hijr: 6] [[Surat al-Hijr, vol. 10, p. 4.]]. Its response is in another surah: ﴿By the favour of your Lord, you are not a madman﴾ [al-Qalam: 2] [[Surat al-Qalam, vol. 18, p. 253.]]. The meaning of the sentence is: "I swear by the Day of Resurrection." This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr and Abu 'Ubayda, and similar to it is the words of the poet:

*I remembered Layla, and passion overcame me,*
*so that the core of my heart nearly was cut to pieces.*

Abu al-Layth al-Samarqandi related: The exegetes agreed that the meaning of "la uqsimu" is "uqsimu" (I swear). They differed over the explanation of "la." Some of them said: "la" is an addition to the speech for embellishment, and the addition of "la" occurs in the Arabic language, as in another verse: ﴿He said, "O Iblis, what prevented you from prostrating?"﴾ [Sad: 75], meaning "from prostrating." Others said: "la" is a rejection of their statement, since they denied the Resurrection, so He says: "The matter is not as you claim." I say: This is the view of al-Farra'. Al-Farra' said: Many grammarians say that "la" is a redundant particle, but it is not permissible to begin with a negation and then make it redundant, because if that were so, a statement containing a negation could not be distinguished from a statement without negation. Rather, the Qur'an came to refute those who denied the Resurrection, the Garden and the Fire, so the oath came as a refutation of them [in much of speech that begins with it and in that which does not begin with it] [[The addition is from the tafsir of al-Farra'.]]. This is like their saying: "No, by God, I will not do it," where "la" is a rejection of a statement that has already passed. It is like your saying: "No, by God, the Resurrection is indeed true," as if you were denying a people who rejected it. Someone other than al-Farra' recited for Imru' al-Qays:

*No, by your father, daughter of al-'Amiri,*
*the people shall not claim that I flee.*

Ghuwayya ibn Sulma said:

*Umama called out, carrying [her load] away, to grieve me;*
*no, by you, I do not care.*

Its benefit is the emphasis of the oath in the refutation. Al-Farra' said: Whoever does not know this aspect recites "la-uqsimu" without an alif, as if it were the lam of emphasis (lam al-ta'kid) that entered upon "uqsimu." This is correct, because the Arabs say "la-uqsimu billah." This is the reading of al-Hasan, Ibn Kathir, al-Zuhri and Ibn Humruz. ﴿by the Day of Resurrection﴾, meaning by a day on which people will stand before their Lord. It is permissible for God, Mighty and Majestic, to swear by whatever He wishes.

(﴿And I swear by the self-reproaching soul﴾) There is no disagreement among the readers about this: He, glory be to Him, swore by the Day of Resurrection to magnify its matter [and He did not swear by the soul [[The addition is from the tafsir of Ibn 'Atiyya and others.]]]. According to the reading of Ibn Kathir, He swore by the first and did not swear by the second. It has been said: "And I swear by the self-reproaching soul" is another refutation and the beginning of an oath by the self-reproaching soul. Al-Tha'labi said: The correct view is that He swore by both of them together. The meaning of "by the self-reproaching soul" is by the soul of the believer, who, whenever you see him, reproaches himself, saying: "What did I intend by such-and-such?" You will see him only rebuking his own soul. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Hasan and others. Al-Hasan said: By God, it is the soul of the believer; the believer is seen only reproaching himself: "What did I intend by my speech? What did I intend by my eating? What did I intend by my inner talk?" The wicked does not hold himself to account. Mujahid said: It is the soul that blames itself for what has passed and regrets it; it blames itself for evil, asking why it did it, and for good, asking why it did not increase it. It has been said: it means the one who blames. It has been said: it blames itself for what it blames others for. According to these views, "al-lawwama" carries the meaning of "al-la'ima" (the one who blames), which is a description of praise, and on this basis the oath by it is appropriate and fine. In some exegesis it is said: Adam, peace be upon him, never ceased to blame himself for his disobedience by which he was expelled from the Garden. It has also been said: "al-lawwama" means "al-malumah al-madhumah" (the one blamed and censured), also from Ibn 'Abbas. Then it is a description of blame, and this is the view of those who deny that it is an oath, since a disobedient person has no standing by which one could swear; so it is one that is very much blamed. Muqatil said: It is the soul of the unbeliever who blames himself and grieves in the Hereafter over what he neglected regarding God's right. Al-Farra' said: There is no soul, whether good or bad, but that it blames itself: the one who does good blames himself that he did not increase his good, and the one who does evil blames himself that he did not refrain from his evil.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Does man think that We will not assemble his bones?﴾ That We will restore them to a new creation after they have become dust. Al-Zajjaj said: I swear by the Day of Resurrection and by the self-reproaching soul: He will certainly assemble the bones for the Resurrection, and this is the response of the oath. Al-Nahhas said: The response of the oath is omitted, meaning "you will certainly be raised," and it is indicated by the words of the Exalted: ﴿Does man think that We will not assemble his bones?﴾, for revival and resurrection. Here "man" means the unbeliever who denies the Resurrection. The verse was revealed concerning 'Adi ibn Rabi'a, who said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Tell me about the Day of Resurrection: when will it be, and what is its matter and state?" The Prophet (ﷺ) informed him of that, and he said: "If I were to witness that day, O Muhammad, I would not believe you, nor would I have faith in it, or would God assemble the bones?!" For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) used to say: "O God, suffice me against the evil neighbours, 'Adi ibn Rabi'a and al-Akhnas ibn Shariq." It has also been said: it was revealed concerning the enemy of God, Abu Jahl, when he denied resurrection after death. He mentioned the bones, and what is meant is the whole of him, because the bones are the frame of the creation. ﴿Yes﴾ is a good pause, then you begin with ﴿able﴾. **Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 75, verses 7–13:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So when the sight is dazzled﴾. Nafi' and Abban from ʿAsim read (baraqa) with a fatha on the rāʾ. Its meaning: his sight shone from the intensity of its staring, so you see him not blinking. Mujahid and others said: this is at the time of death. Al-Hasan said: this is on the Day of Resurrection. It carries the sense of an answer to what the human asked about, as if the meaning were: on the Day of Resurrection, "when the sight is dazzled." And "the moon is eclipsed." The rest read (bariqa) with a kasra, and its meaning is: he was bewildered and did not blink. This was stated by Abu ʿAmr, al-Zajjaj and others. Dhu al-Rummah said:

*"Even if Luqman the wise were confronted*
*by a woman of Mayy unveiled, his eyes would nearly be dazzled."*

Al-Farra' and al-Khalil said: bariqa with a kasra means he was alarmed, stunned and bewildered. The Arabs say of a bewildered, stunned person: "He has become baraq (dazzled), so he is baraq." Al-Farra' recited:

*"Be content with yourself and do not tire, and treat the wounds, and do not be dazzled."*

[The speaker is Tarafah.]

That is, do not be alarmed by the multitude of wounds that are on you. It was also said: baraqa yabraqu with a fatha means he split open his eyes and opened them wide. This was stated by Abu ʿUbaydah, who recited the verse of al-Kilabi:

*"When Ibn ʿUmayr came to me seeking, I gave him a camel of mixed white and red, so he opened his eyes wide."*

[In other than al-Qurtubi's text: "When Ibn Subayh came to me." The ʿIs al-Sabaab are camels whose whiteness is mixed with redness, and they are counted among the noblest of camels by the Arabs.]

That is, he opened his eyes. It was also said that the kasra and fatha of the rāʾ are two dialects with the same meaning.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the moon is eclipsed﴾, that is, its light has gone. The eclipse in this world is temporary until it clears, unlike in the Hereafter, when its light will not return. It may also mean that it set, and from this is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So We caused the earth to swallow him and his home﴾ [al-Qasas: 81]. Ibn Abi Ishaq, ʿIsa and al-Aʿraj read (wa-khusifa al-qamar), with a damma on the khāʾ and a kasra on the sīn, and this is indicated by "and the sun and the moon are joined." Abu Hatim Muhammad ibn Idris said: when part of it goes, it is kusuf (partial eclipse), and when all of it goes, it is khusuf (total eclipse). ("And the sun and the moon are joined") means they are joined together in the going of their light, so there is no light for the sun just as there is no light for the moon after its eclipse. This was stated by al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj. Al-Farra' said: he did not say "were joined" (feminine), because the meaning is "joined together." Abu ʿUbaydah said: it is by giving precedence to the masculine. Al-Kisa'i said: it is carried on the meaning, as if he said "the two lights." Al-Mubarrad said: the feminine is not real (grammatically genuine). Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Masʿud said: they are joined together, meaning they are coupled together in their rising from the west, black, folded up, darkened, coupled, as if they were two bulls with their legs hobbled. The hadith with this meaning has already passed at the end of Surah al-Anʿam [see vol. 7, p. 146]. In the reading of ʿAbdullah: "and the sun and the moon were joined." ʿAta' ibn Yasar said: they will be joined together on the Day of Resurrection, then they will be cast into the sea, and they will be the Great Fire of God. ʿAli and Ibn ʿAbbas said: they will be placed in the light of the veils [the addition is from the books of tafsir]. They may also be joined in the fire of Hell, because they were worshipped besides God, and the fire will not be a punishment for them, since they are inanimate. It is done to them only as an increase in the rebuke and regret of the disbelievers. In the Musnad of Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi, from Yazid al-Raqashi, from Anas ibn Malik, raising it to the Prophet (ﷺ), he said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Indeed the sun and the moon are two bulls with their legs hobbled in the Fire." It was also said: this joining means that they come together and do not separate, and they draw near to the people, so sweat overtakes them because of the intense heat; so the meaning is that their heat is gathered upon them. It was also said: the sun and the moon are joined, so there is no alternation of night and day there.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿On that day the human will say: where is the escape?﴾ That is, the son of Adam will say, and it is said [it refers to] Abu Jahl: where is the place of escape? The poet said:

*"Where is the escape, when the rams clash,*
*and which ram that swerves from them will not be disgraced?"*

Al-Mawardi said: it may bear two meanings. The first: where is the escape from God, out of shame before Him. The second: where is the escape from Hell, out of fear of it. This statement from the human may be of two kinds. The first: that it is specifically from the disbeliever at the moment of the Resurrection, not the believer, because of the believer's confidence in the good news from his Lord. The second: that it is the statement of both the believer and the disbeliever at the establishment of the Hour, because of the terror of what they witness of it. The reading of the common people is "al-maffar" with a fatha on the fāʾ, and Abu ʿUbaydah and Abu Hatim chose it, because it is a verbal noun (maṣdar). Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, al-Hasan and Qatadah read it with a kasra on the fāʾ and a fatha on the mīm. Al-Kisa'i said: they are two dialects, like madabb and madibb, and maṣahh and maṣih. From al-Zuhri: with a kasra on the mīm and a fatha on the fāʾ. Al-Mahdawi [al-Mahdawi, a Qur'an scholar]: whoever reads with a fatha on both the mīm and the fāʾ, "al-maffar" is a verbal noun meaning the act of fleeing; whoever reads with a fatha on the mīm and a kasra on the fāʾ, it is the place to which one flees; and whoever reads with a kasra on the mīm and a fatha on the fāʾ, it is the person who is skilled at fleeing, so the meaning is: where is the person skilled at fleeing, and he will not be saved despite that. I say: from this is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*"Skilled in attack and retreat, advancing and withdrawing together."* [The complete line: "Like a boulder of rock that the flood has cast down from a height."]

He means that he is good at attack and at flight.

(Kalla): that is, no escape. Kalla is a rejection, and it is from the word of God, may He be exalted. Then He explained this rejection by saying: ﴿No refuge﴾, that is, no shelter from the Fire. Ibn Masʿud used to say: no fortress. al-Hasan used to say: no mountain. Ibn ʿAbbas said: no shelter. Ibn Jubayr: no escape and no protection. The meaning in all of this is one. In language, al-wazar is what one takes refuge in, whether a fortress, a mountain, or something else. The poet said:

*"By my life, there is no refuge for a youth*
*from death, which overtakes him, or from old age."*

al-Suddi said: in the world, when they were frightened they would take refuge in the mountains, so God said to them: there is no refuge that will protect you from Me that day. Tarafah said:

*"Bakr certainly knows that we*
*are excellent in judgment and in the moment of terror, a refuge."*

That is, a shelter for the one who fears. It is also transmitted as "waqr" (weight/dignity).

(﴿To your Lord that day is the resting place﴾)

That is, the final destination. Qatadah said this. Its parallel is: ﴿And that to your Lord is the final end﴾ [al-Najm: 42]. Ibn Masʿud said: ﴿To your Lord is the return and the place of return﴾. It was said: that is, the place of rest in the Hereafter, where God causes it to rest, since He is the judge among them. It was also said: "Kalla" is the statement of the human to himself when he knows there is no escape for him, so he says to himself: "No, there is no refuge. To your Lord, that day, is the resting place."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The human will be informed﴾, that is, the son of Adam will be informed, whether righteous or wicked, ﴿of what he sent forward and put off﴾. That is: of what he had sent ahead of evil or good deeds, or put off of an evil or good practice that is followed after him. This was stated by Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Masʿud. Mansur related from Mujahid that he said: he will be informed of his first deed and his last. This was also said by al-Nakhaʿi. Ibn ʿAbbas also said: that is, of what he sent forward of disobedience, and put off of obedience. This is the view of Qatadah.

Ibn Zayd said: ﴿of what he sent forward﴾ of his wealth for himself, and ﴿put off﴾: left behind for the heirs. al-Dahhak said: he will be informed of what he sent forward of obligation, and put off of obligation. al-Qushayri said: this informing will occur on the Day of Resurrection at the weighing of deeds, and it may be at the time of death. I say: the first is more evident, because of what Ibn Majah recorded in his Sunan from the hadith of al-Zuhri: Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Aghurr related to me from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Among what reaches the believer from his deeds and good works after his death is knowledge that he taught and spread, and a righteous child he left behind, or a copy of the Qur'an he bequeathed, or a mosque he built, or a house he built for the traveller, or a river he caused to flow, or charity he gave from his wealth in his health and life, which reaches him after his death." Abu Nuʿaym al-Hafiz also recorded it in meaning from the hadith of Qatadah, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Seven things whose reward continues for the servant after his death, while he is in his grave: one who taught knowledge, or caused a river to flow, or dug a well, or planted a palm tree, or built a mosque, or bequeathed a copy of the Qur'an, or left a child who seeks forgiveness for him after his death." His saying: "after his death, while he is in his grave" is an explicit statement that this does not occur at the time of death, but that he is informed of all of that at the weighing of his deeds, although he is given good news of it in his grave. This is also indicated by the Truth's saying: ﴿And they will surely bear their burdens and burdens along with their burdens﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 13] (see vol. 13, p. 330), and His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And of the burdens of those who lead them astray without knowledge﴾ [al-Nahl: 25] (see vol. 10, p. 96). This is not but in the Hereafter after the weighing of deeds. And God knows best.

His saying: "after his death, while he is in his grave" is an explicit statement that this does not occur at the time of death, but that he is informed of all of that at the weighing of his deeds, although he is given good news of it in his grave. This is also indicated by the Truth's saying: ﴿And they will surely bear their burdens and burdens along with their burdens﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 13] (see vol. 13, p. 330), and His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And of the burdens of those who lead them astray without knowledge﴾ [al-Nahl: 25] (see vol. 10, p. 96). This is not but in the Hereafter after the weighing of deeds. And God knows best.

In the Sahih: "Whoever establishes a good practice in Islam, he will have its reward and the reward of whoever acts upon it after him, without anything being diminished from their rewards; and whoever establishes an evil practice in Islam, he will bear its burden and the burden of whoever acts upon it after him, without anything being diminished from their burdens."

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 75, verses 7–13:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So when the sight is dazzled﴾. Nafi' and Abban from ʿAsim read (baraqa) with a fatha on the rāʾ. Its meaning: his sight shone from the intensity of its staring, so you see him not blinking. Mujahid and others said: this is at the time of death. Al-Hasan said: this is on the Day of Resurrection. It carries the sense of an answer to what the human asked about, as if the meaning were: on the Day of Resurrection, "when the sight is dazzled." And "the moon is eclipsed." The rest read (bariqa) with a kasra, and its meaning is: he was bewildered and did not blink. This was stated by Abu ʿAmr, al-Zajjaj and others. Dhu al-Rummah said:

*"Even if Luqman the wise were confronted*
*by a woman of Mayy unveiled, his eyes would nearly be dazzled."*

Al-Farra' and al-Khalil said: bariqa with a kasra means he was alarmed, stunned and bewildered. The Arabs say of a bewildered, stunned person: "He has become baraq (dazzled), so he is baraq." Al-Farra' recited:

*"Be content with yourself and do not tire, and treat the wounds, and do not be dazzled."*

[The speaker is Tarafah.]

That is, do not be alarmed by the multitude of wounds that are on you. It was also said: baraqa yabraqu with a fatha means he split open his eyes and opened them wide. This was stated by Abu ʿUbaydah, who recited the verse of al-Kilabi:

*"When Ibn ʿUmayr came to me seeking, I gave him a camel of mixed white and red, so he opened his eyes wide."*

[In other than al-Qurtubi's text: "When Ibn Subayh came to me." The ʿIs al-Sabaab are camels whose whiteness is mixed with redness, and they are counted among the noblest of camels by the Arabs.]

That is, he opened his eyes. It was also said that the kasra and fatha of the rāʾ are two dialects with the same meaning.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the moon is eclipsed﴾, that is, its light has gone. The eclipse in this world is temporary until it clears, unlike in the Hereafter, when its light will not return. It may also mean that it set, and from this is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So We caused the earth to swallow him and his home﴾ [al-Qasas: 81]. Ibn Abi Ishaq, ʿIsa and al-Aʿraj read (wa-khusifa al-qamar), with a damma on the khāʾ and a kasra on the sīn, and this is indicated by "and the sun and the moon are joined." Abu Hatim Muhammad ibn Idris said: when part of it goes, it is kusuf (partial eclipse), and when all of it goes, it is khusuf (total eclipse). ("And the sun and the moon are joined") means they are joined together in the going of their light, so there is no light for the sun just as there is no light for the moon after its eclipse. This was stated by al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj. Al-Farra' said: he did not say "were joined" (feminine), because the meaning is "joined together." Abu ʿUbaydah said: it is by giving precedence to the masculine. Al-Kisa'i said: it is carried on the meaning, as if he said "the two lights." Al-Mubarrad said: the feminine is not real (grammatically genuine). Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Masʿud said: they are joined together, meaning they are coupled together in their rising from the west, black, folded up, darkened, coupled, as if they were two bulls with their legs hobbled. The hadith with this meaning has already passed at the end of Surah al-Anʿam [see vol. 7, p. 146]. In the reading of ʿAbdullah: "and the sun and the moon were joined." ʿAta' ibn Yasar said: they will be joined together on the Day of Resurrection, then they will be cast into the sea, and they will be the Great Fire of God. ʿAli and Ibn ʿAbbas said: they will be placed in the light of the veils [the addition is from the books of tafsir]. They may also be joined in the fire of Hell, because they were worshipped besides God, and the fire will not be a punishment for them, since they are inanimate. It is done to them only as an increase in the rebuke and regret of the disbelievers. In the Musnad of Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi, from Yazid al-Raqashi, from Anas ibn Malik, raising it to the Prophet (ﷺ), he said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Indeed the sun and the moon are two bulls with their legs hobbled in the Fire." It was also said: this joining means that they come together and do not separate, and they draw near to the people, so sweat overtakes them because of the intense heat; so the meaning is that their heat is gathered upon them. It was also said: the sun and the moon are joined, so there is no alternation of night and day there.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿On that day the human will say: where is the escape?﴾ That is, the son of Adam will say, and it is said [it refers to] Abu Jahl: where is the place of escape? The poet said:

*"Where is the escape, when the rams clash,*
*and which ram that swerves from them will not be disgraced?"*

Al-Mawardi said: it may bear two meanings. The first: where is the escape from God, out of shame before Him. The second: where is the escape from Hell, out of fear of it. This statement from the human may be of two kinds. The first: that it is specifically from the disbeliever at the moment of the Resurrection, not the believer, because of the believer's confidence in the good news from his Lord. The second: that it is the statement of both the believer and the disbeliever at the establishment of the Hour, because of the terror of what they witness of it. The reading of the common people is "al-maffar" with a fatha on the fāʾ, and Abu ʿUbaydah and Abu Hatim chose it, because it is a verbal noun (maṣdar). Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, al-Hasan and Qatadah read it with a kasra on the fāʾ and a fatha on the mīm. Al-Kisa'i said: they are two dialects, like madabb and madibb, and maṣahh and maṣih. From al-Zuhri: with a kasra on the mīm and a fatha on the fāʾ. Al-Mahdawi [al-Mahdawi, a Qur'an scholar]: whoever reads with a fatha on both the mīm and the fāʾ, "al-maffar" is a verbal noun meaning the act of fleeing; whoever reads with a fatha on the mīm and a kasra on the fāʾ, it is the place to which one flees; and whoever reads with a kasra on the mīm and a fatha on the fāʾ, it is the person who is skilled at fleeing, so the meaning is: where is the person skilled at fleeing, and he will not be saved despite that. I say: from this is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*"Skilled in attack and retreat, advancing and withdrawing together."* [The complete line: "Like a boulder of rock that the flood has cast down from a height."]

He means that he is good at attack and at flight.

(Kalla): that is, no escape. Kalla is a rejection, and it is from the word of God, may He be exalted. Then He explained this rejection by saying: ﴿No refuge﴾, that is, no shelter from the Fire. Ibn Masʿud used to say: no fortress. al-Hasan used to say: no mountain. Ibn ʿAbbas said: no shelter. Ibn Jubayr: no escape and no protection. The meaning in all of this is one. In language, al-wazar is what one takes refuge in, whether a fortress, a mountain, or something else. The poet said:

*"By my life, there is no refuge for a youth*
*from death, which overtakes him, or from old age."*

al-Suddi said: in the world, when they were frightened they would take refuge in the mountains, so God said to them: there is no refuge that will protect you from Me that day. Tarafah said:

*"Bakr certainly knows that we*
*are excellent in judgment and in the moment of terror, a refuge."*

That is, a shelter for the one who fears. It is also transmitted as "waqr" (weight/dignity).

(﴿To your Lord that day is the resting place﴾)

That is, the final destination. Qatadah said this. Its parallel is: ﴿And that to your Lord is the final end﴾ [al-Najm: 42]. Ibn Masʿud said: ﴿To your Lord is the return and the place of return﴾. It was said: that is, the place of rest in the Hereafter, where God causes it to rest, since He is the judge among them. It was also said: "Kalla" is the statement of the human to himself when he knows there is no escape for him, so he says to himself: "No, there is no refuge. To your Lord, that day, is the resting place."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The human will be informed﴾, that is, the son of Adam will be informed, whether righteous or wicked, ﴿of what he sent forward and put off﴾. That is: of what he had sent ahead of evil or good deeds, or put off of an evil or good practice that is followed after him. This was stated by Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Masʿud. Mansur related from Mujahid that he said: he will be informed of his first deed and his last. This was also said by al-Nakhaʿi. Ibn ʿAbbas also said: that is, of what he sent forward of disobedience, and put off of obedience. This is the view of Qatadah.

Ibn Zayd said: ﴿of what he sent forward﴾ of his wealth for himself, and ﴿put off﴾: left behind for the heirs. al-Dahhak said: he will be informed of what he sent forward of obligation, and put off of obligation. al-Qushayri said: this informing will occur on the Day of Resurrection at the weighing of deeds, and it may be at the time of death. I say: the first is more evident, because of what Ibn Majah recorded in his Sunan from the hadith of al-Zuhri: Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Aghurr related to me from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Among what reaches the believer from his deeds and good works after his death is knowledge that he taught and spread, and a righteous child he left behind, or a copy of the Qur'an he bequeathed, or a mosque he built, or a house he built for the traveller, or a river he caused to flow, or charity he gave from his wealth in his health and life, which reaches him after his death." Abu Nuʿaym al-Hafiz also recorded it in meaning from the hadith of Qatadah, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Seven things whose reward continues for the servant after his death, while he is in his grave: one who taught knowledge, or caused a river to flow, or dug a well, or planted a palm tree, or built a mosque, or bequeathed a copy of the Qur'an, or left a child who seeks forgiveness for him after his death." His saying: "after his death, while he is in his grave" is an explicit statement that this does not occur at the time of death, but that he is informed of all of that at the weighing of his deeds, although he is given good news of it in his grave. This is also indicated by the Truth's saying: ﴿And they will surely bear their burdens and burdens along with their burdens﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 13] (see vol. 13, p. 330), and His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And of the burdens of those who lead them astray without knowledge﴾ [al-Nahl: 25] (see vol. 10, p. 96). This is not but in the Hereafter after the weighing of deeds. And God knows best.

In the Sahih: "Whoever establishes a good practice in Islam, he will have its reward and the reward of whoever acts upon it after him, without anything being diminished from their rewards; and whoever establishes an evil practice in Islam, he will bear its burden and the burden of whoever acts upon it after him, without anything being diminished from their burdens."

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 75, verses 14–15 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Nay, man is a witness against himself﴾.

Al-Akhfash said: He made him (man) himself the *basirah* (witness), as you say to a man, "You are a proof against yourself." Ibn 'Abbas said: *basirah* means a witness (*shahid*), namely the testimony of his limbs against him: his hands for what they seized, his feet for where they walked, and his eyes for what they saw. *Al-basirah* means the witness. Al-Farra' recited:

*As if over the one of intellect there is a seeing eye,*
*Watching his place of sitting, or whatever sight he looks upon.*
*He is wary, until he thinks all people,*
*Out of fear, cannot conceal his inner secrets from them.*

The evidence for this interpretation from the Revelation is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿On the Day when their tongues, their hands and their feet will bear witness against them concerning what they used to do﴾ [al-Nur: 24]. [See vol. 12, p. 210.]

The feminine form *basirah* came because the intended meaning of "man" here is the limbs, since they are witnesses against the self of man. It is as if He said: "Nay, the limbs are a *basirah* against the self of man." This was said by al-Qutabi and others.

Some people say that the *ha'* in His saying *basirah* is what the grammarians call *ha' al-mubalaghah* (the *ha'* of intensification), like the *ha'* in their words *dahiyah* (calamity), *allamah* (very learned) and *rawiyah* (very prolific transmitter). This is the view of Abu 'Ubayd.

It has also been said that *al-basirah* means the two recording angels who write down whatever good or evil he does. The evidence for this is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Even if he should put forth his excuses﴾. This is according to those who understand *al-ma'adhir* to mean "the veils." This is the view of al-Suddi and al-Dahhak.

Some of the exegetes said: The meaning is "Nay, against man from himself is a *basirah*," i.e., a witness, and the preposition has been omitted.

It is also permissible for *basirah* to be an adjective (*na't*) of a feminine noun, so that its implied construction is: "Nay, man against his self is a seeing eye (*ayn basirah*)." Al-Farra' recited:

*As if over the one of intellect there is a seeing eye.*

Al-Hasan said concerning His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Nay, man against himself is a basirah﴾: He means that he is perceptive regarding the faults of others, but ignorant of the faults of himself.

(﴿Even if he should put forth his excuses﴾): That is, even if he should let down his veils. *Al-mi'dhar* in the dialect of the people of Yemen means a veil. This was said by al-Dahhak. A poet said:

*But she (the abode) withheld from us a moment's dwelling,*
*And she (the camel) hastened above it with the veils.*

Al-Zajjaj said: *al-ma'adhir* means veils, and its singular is *mi'dhar*. That is: even if he lets down his veil, wishing to conceal his deed, his own self is a witness against him. It has also been said: That is, even if he makes an excuse and says, "I did nothing," there would still be against him a witness from himself, namely his limbs. Thus, although he makes excuses and argues on behalf of himself, there is a witness against him that refutes his excuse. This was said by Mujahid, Qatadah, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd, Abu al-'Aliyah, 'Ata', al-Farra', also al-Suddi, and Muqatil. Muqatil said: That is, even if he presents an excuse or argument, it will not benefit him. Its parallel is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿On the Day when the excuses of the wrongdoers will not benefit them﴾ [Ghafir: 52], and His saying: ﴿Nor will they be permitted to make excuses﴾ [al-Mursalat: 36]. According to this view, *al-ma'adhir* is derived from *al-'udhr* (excuse). A poet said:

*Beware of a matter which, if its sources widen,*
*Its outlets become narrow upon you.*
*So it is not good for a man to excuse himself,*
*When he has no excuser among all people.*

A man made an excuse to Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, and he said to him: "I have excused you without you being excused, for excuses are mixed with falsehood." Ibn 'Abbas said concerning ﴿even if he should put forth his excuses﴾: That is, even if he were stripped of his garments. This was related by al-Mawardi.

I say: The more apparent meaning is that it refers to presenting proof and offering an excuse for a sin. From this is the saying of al-Nabighah:

*Indeed, the one with an excuse, unless it benefits him,*
*Then its owner is a partner in the distress.*

The evidence for this is His saying, Exalted is He, concerning the disbelievers: ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ [al-An'am: 23], and His saying concerning the hypocrites: ﴿On the Day when Allah will raise them all, and they will swear to Him as they swear to you﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 18]. [See vol. 17, p. 982.] It is in the Sahih that he will say: "O Lord, I believed in You, and in Your Book, and in Your Messenger; I prayed, I fasted, and I gave charity," and he will praise himself with whatever good he is able to. [The hadith is related in full ...] This has been mentioned previously in "Ha Mim, the Prostration" [[See vol. 15, p. 35, where there is a meaning of what al-Qurtubi indicated here. As for the hadith, he cited it in surah al-An'am, vol. 6, p. 402.]] and elsewhere.

*Al-ma'adhir* and *al-ma'adhir* are the plural of *ma'dhirah* (excuse). It is said: "I excused him regarding what he did, I excuse him, an excuse (*'udhr*) and *'udhur*," and the noun is *al-ma'dhirah* and *al-'udhri*. The poet said: [The sayer of this is al-Jumuh al-Zafari. It is also said he is Rashid ibn 'Abd Rabbih. *'Udhri* is a shortened form. In al-Lisan the correct recitation is *lawla hiddittu* (if only I had been restricted), with the intended meaning that the phrase should be "lawla an hiddittu," because *lawla*, which means the non-occurrence of one thing due to the existence of another, is restricted to nouns, though verbs may follow it in the sense of *an*.]

*Indeed I have been restricted, and no excuse of mine*
*Is acceptable for one who is restricted.*

Likewise, *al-'udhrah* is similar to *al-rukbah* and *al-jilsah* (forms of nouns). Al-Nabighah said:

*Indeed, if the one with an excuse, unless it benefits him,*
*Then its owner has wandered in the land.* [[The verse was cited earlier with the variant: "Indeed, the one ... its partner in the distress." These are two transmissions.]]

This verse contains five issues.

**The first issue:** Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi (al-Qadi) said: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Nay, man is a witness against himself, even if he should put forth his excuses﴾, contains evidence that a person's acknowledgement (*iqrar*) against himself is accepted, because it is a testimony from him against himself. Allah, Glorified and Exalted is He, said: ﴿On the Day when their tongues, their hands and their feet will bear witness against them concerning what they used to do﴾ [al-Nur: 24]. There is no disagreement about this, because it is a report in a manner that removes suspicion from him, since a sane person does not lie against himself. This is the matter. Indeed, Allah, Glorified is He, said in His Noble Book: ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of the Prophets: "Whatever I have given you of Scripture and wisdom, and then there comes to you a Messenger confirming what you have, you must believe in him and support him." He said: "Do you affirm and accept My commitment on that?" They said: "We affirm it." He said: "Then bear witness, and I am with you among the witnesses"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 81]. Then He, Exalted, said: ﴿And others have acknowledged their sins; they mixed a righteous deed with another that was evil﴾ [al-Tawbah: 102]. [See vol. 4, p. 124; vol. 8, p. 240.] There are many such reports. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Go out in the morning, O Unays, to the wife of this man, and if she confesses, then stone her." As for the acknowledgement of one party against another regarding an heir or a debt, Malik said: "The matter agreed upon among us regarding a man who dies leaving sons, and one of them says: 'My father acknowledged that so-and-so is his son,' is that this lineage is not established by the testimony of a single person, and the acknowledgement of the one who acknowledged is not valid except against himself regarding his share of his father's property. The one to whom testimony was given is given the amount of the debt which falls to him from the property in the hand of [the one who acknowledged]." Malik said: The explanation of that is that a man dies leaving two sons and six hundred dinars, then one of them testifies that his deceased father acknowledged that so-and-so is his son. Then the one who testified owes the one who is entitled one hundred dinars, which is half the inheritance of the acknowledged son if he had been established. If the other also acknowledges him, he takes the other hundred, completing his right, and his lineage is established. This is also similar to a woman who acknowledges a debt owed by her father or by her husband, and the heirs deny it. She must pay to the one to whom she acknowledged the amount that would fall to her from that debt if it were established against all the heirs. If she is a wife who inherits an eighth, she pays the creditor an eighth of his debt; if she is a daughter who inherits a half, she pays the creditor a half of his debt. On this reckoning, women who acknowledge pay what they owe.

**The third issue:** An acknowledgement is valid only from a legally responsible person (*mukallaf*), on condition that he is not under restriction (*mahjur 'alayhi*), because restriction nullifies his statement if it concerns his own right. If it concerns the right of another, as with a sick person, his statement is partly void and partly valid. Its explanation belongs in the books of jurisprudence. A slave has two situations regarding acknowledgement: the first at its beginning, and there is no disagreement about it in the manner already mentioned. The second is at its conclusion, such as the ambiguity of acknowledgement. It has many forms, and its principal forms are six.

The first form: that he says to him, "I have something (*shay'*)." Al-Shafi'i said: If he explains it as a date or a piece of bread, it is accepted from him. What our principles require is that it is not accepted except for what has a value. When he explains it with that, it is accepted from him and he takes an oath regarding it.

The second form: that he explains it as wine, pork, or what is not property in the Law. It is not accepted by agreement, even if the one to whom it was acknowledged agrees with him on it.

The third form: that he explains it with something disputed, such as the hide of a carrion, dung, or a dog. [The judge rules on it according to what he sees, whether to reject or to uphold.] If he rejects it, no other judge may rule against him in anything, because the ruling has been carried out by annulling it. Some companions of al-Shafi'i said: wine and pork are binding; this is a false view. Abu Hanifah said: If he says, "I owe him something," his explanation is not accepted except as something measured or weighed, because only these two are established in the liability by themselves. This is weak, for other things are established in liability when they are due, by consensus.

The fourth form: if he says to him, "I have property," his explanation is accepted as what is not property in customary usage, such as a dirham or two dirhams, unless circumstantial evidence comes which would justify ruling for more than that.

The fifth form: that he says to him, "I have much property" or "great property." Al-Shafi'i said: It is accepted for a grain. Abu Hanifah said: It is not accepted except for the minimum of the zakat threshold (*nisab*). Our scholars held various views regarding this, among them the threshold of theft, of zakat, and of blood-money. The least of these in my view is the threshold of theft, because the limb of a Muslim is not cut off except for great property. This is also the view of most Hanafis. Whoever is astonished at the view of al-Layth ibn Sa'd, that it is not accepted for less than seventy-two dirhams, and was asked, "From where do you say that?" He said: Because Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Allah has already given you victory on many occasions, and on the Day of Hunayn﴾ [al-Tawbah: 25], and His military expeditions and raids were seventy-two. This is not sound, because he excluded Hunayn from them, and his proper statement would have been that it is accepted for seventy-one. Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Remember Allah with much remembrance﴾ [al-Ahzab: 41], and He said: ﴿There is no good in much of their secret talk﴾ [al-Nisa': 114], and He said: ﴿And curse them with a great curse﴾ [al-Ahzab: 68]. [The text of the hadith and report is omitted in the source.]

The sixth form: if he says to him, "I owe ten, or a hundred, or a thousand," he explains them with whatever he wishes and it is accepted from him. If he says "a thousand dirhams," or "a hundred and a slave," or "a hundred and fifty dirhams," he explains the ambiguous quantity and it is accepted from him. This is also the view of al-Shafi'i. Abu Hanifah said: If he joins to the indefinite number something measured or weighed, it counts as an explanation, as in his saying "a hundred and fifty dirhams," because the dirham is an explanation of the fifty, and the fifty is an explanation of the hundred. Ibn Kharan al-Istakhri, one of al-Shafi'i's companions, said: The dirham is not an explanation of the hundred and fifty except for the fifty alone, and he explains the hundred with whatever he wishes.

**The fourth issue:** His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Even if he should put forth his excuses﴾.

Its meaning: if he retracts after confessing, his retraction is not accepted from him. The scholars differed concerning one who retracts after confessing to the hudud (penal punishments) which are the exclusive right of God. Most of them, including al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifa, said: his retraction is accepted after the confession. Malik also held this in one of his two opinions, and in the other opinion he said: it is not accepted unless he mentions a valid reason for his retraction. The correct view is that retraction is permissible without qualification, based on what the imams, including al-Bukhari and Muslim, narrated: that the Prophet ﷺ turned away the one who confessed to adultery several times, four times, each time turning away from him. When he testified against himself four times, the Prophet ﷺ summoned him and said: (Are you insane?) He said: No. He said: (Are you married?) He said: Yes. In the hadith of al-Bukhari: (Perhaps you kissed, or touched, or looked). In al-Nasa'i and Abu Dawud: until he said to him in the fifth (Did you have intercourse with her?) He said: Yes. He said: (Until that disappeared from you into that in her?) He said: Yes. He said: (Just as the kohl stick disappears into the kohl pot and the rope into the well). He said: Yes. Then he said: (Do you know what adultery is?) He said: Yes, I had with her what a man has with his wife lawfully. He said: (What then do you want from me?) He said: I want you to purify me. So he ordered him and he was stoned. Al-Tirmidhi and Abu Dawud said: when he felt the touch of the stones, he fled running. A man struck him with a jawbone of a camel, and the people struck him until he died. The Prophet ﷺ said: (Why did you not leave him?) **Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 75, verses 14–15 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Nay, man is a witness against himself﴾.

Al-Akhfash said: He made him (man) himself the *basirah* (witness), as you say to a man, "You are a proof against yourself." Ibn 'Abbas said: *basirah* means a witness (*shahid*), namely the testimony of his limbs against him: his hands for what they seized, his feet for where they walked, and his eyes for what they saw. *Al-basirah* means the witness. Al-Farra' recited:

*As if over the one of intellect there is a seeing eye,*
*Watching his place of sitting, or whatever sight he looks upon.*
*He is wary, until he thinks all people,*
*Out of fear, cannot conceal his inner secrets from them.*

The evidence for this interpretation from the Revelation is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿On the Day when their tongues, their hands and their feet will bear witness against them concerning what they used to do﴾ [al-Nur: 24]. [See vol. 12, p. 210.]

The feminine form *basirah* came because the intended meaning of "man" here is the limbs, since they are witnesses against the self of man. It is as if He said: "Nay, the limbs are a *basirah* against the self of man." This was said by al-Qutabi and others.

Some people say that the *ha'* in His saying *basirah* is what the grammarians call *ha' al-mubalaghah* (the *ha'* of intensification), like the *ha'* in their words *dahiyah* (calamity), *allamah* (very learned) and *rawiyah* (very prolific transmitter). This is the view of Abu 'Ubayd.

It has also been said that *al-basirah* means the two recording angels who write down whatever good or evil he does. The evidence for this is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Even if he should put forth his excuses﴾. This is according to those who understand *al-ma'adhir* to mean "the veils." This is the view of al-Suddi and al-Dahhak.

Some of the exegetes said: The meaning is "Nay, against man from himself is a *basirah*," i.e., a witness, and the preposition has been omitted.

It is also permissible for *basirah* to be an adjective (*na't*) of a feminine noun, so that its implied construction is: "Nay, man against his self is a seeing eye (*ayn basirah*)." Al-Farra' recited:

*As if over the one of intellect there is a seeing eye.*

Al-Hasan said concerning His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Nay, man against himself is a basirah﴾: He means that he is perceptive regarding the faults of others, but ignorant of the faults of himself.

(﴿Even if he should put forth his excuses﴾): That is, even if he should let down his veils. *Al-mi'dhar* in the dialect of the people of Yemen means a veil. This was said by al-Dahhak. A poet said:

*But she (the abode) withheld from us a moment's dwelling,*
*And she (the camel) hastened above it with the veils.*

Al-Zajjaj said: *al-ma'adhir* means veils, and its singular is *mi'dhar*. That is: even if he lets down his veil, wishing to conceal his deed, his own self is a witness against him. It has also been said: That is, even if he makes an excuse and says, "I did nothing," there would still be against him a witness from himself, namely his limbs. Thus, although he makes excuses and argues on behalf of himself, there is a witness against him that refutes his excuse. This was said by Mujahid, Qatadah, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd, Abu al-'Aliyah, 'Ata', al-Farra', also al-Suddi, and Muqatil. Muqatil said: That is, even if he presents an excuse or argument, it will not benefit him. Its parallel is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿On the Day when the excuses of the wrongdoers will not benefit them﴾ [Ghafir: 52], and His saying: ﴿Nor will they be permitted to make excuses﴾ [al-Mursalat: 36]. *Beware of a matter which, if its sources widen,*
*Its outlets become narrow upon you.*
*So it is not good for a man to excuse himself,*
*When he has no excuser among all people.*

A man made an excuse to Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, and he said to him: "I have excused you without you being excused, for excuses are mixed with falsehood." Ibn 'Abbas said concerning ﴿even if he should put forth his excuses﴾: That is, even if he were stripped of his garments. This was related by al-Mawardi.

*Indeed, the one with an excuse, unless it benefits him,*
*Then its owner is a partner in the distress.*

The evidence for this is His saying, Exalted is He, concerning the disbelievers: ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ [al-An'am: 23], and His saying concerning the hypocrites: ﴿On the Day when Allah will raise them all, and they will swear to Him as they swear to you﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 18]. [The hadith is related in full ...] This has been mentioned previously in "Ha Mim, the Prostration" [[See vol. 15, p. 35, where there is a meaning of what al-Qurtubi indicated here. As for the hadith, he cited it in surah al-An'am, vol. 6, p. 402.]] and elsewhere.

*Al-ma'adhir* and *al-ma'adhir* are the plural of *ma'dhirah* (excuse). It is said: "I excused him regarding what he did, I excuse him, an excuse (*'udhr*) and *'udhur*," and the noun is *al-ma'dhirah* and *al-'udhri*. The poet said: [The sayer of this is al-Jumuh al-Zafari. It is also said he is Rashid ibn 'Abd Rabbih. *'Udhri* is a shortened form. *Is acceptable for one who is restricted.*

*Then its owner has wandered in the land.* [[The verse was cited earlier with the variant: "Indeed, the one ... its partner in the distress." These are two transmissions.]]

This verse contains five issues.

There is no disagreement about this, because it is a report in a manner that removes suspicion from him, since a sane person does not lie against himself. This is the matter. If she is a wife who inherits an eighth, she pays the creditor an eighth of his debt; if she is a daughter who inherits a half, she pays the creditor a half of his debt. **The third issue:** An acknowledgement is valid only from a legally responsible person (*mukallaf*), on condition that he is not under restriction (*mahjur 'alayhi*), because restriction nullifies his statement if it concerns his own right. If it concerns the right of another, as with a sick person, his statement is partly void and partly valid. Its explanation belongs in the books of jurisprudence. A slave has two situations regarding acknowledgement: the first at its beginning, and there is no disagreement about it in the manner already mentioned. The second is at its conclusion, such as the ambiguity of acknowledgement. It has many forms, and its principal forms are six.

The first form: that he says to him, "I have something (*shay'*)." Al-Shafi'i said: If he explains it as a date or a piece of bread, it is accepted from him. What our principles require is that it is not accepted except for what has a value. When he explains it with that, it is accepted from him and he takes an oath regarding it.

The second form: that he explains it as wine, pork, or what is not property in the Law. It is not accepted by agreement, even if the one to whom it was acknowledged agrees with him on it.

The third form: that he explains it with something disputed, such as the hide of a carrion, dung, or a dog. [The judge rules on it according to what he sees, whether to reject or to uphold.] If he rejects it, no other judge may rule against him in anything, because the ruling has been carried out by annulling it. Some companions of al-Shafi'i said: wine and pork are binding; this is a false view. Abu Hanifah said: If he says, "I owe him something," his explanation is not accepted except as something measured or weighed, because only these two are established in the liability by themselves. This is weak, for other things are established in liability when they are due, by consensus.

The fourth form: if he says to him, "I have property," his explanation is accepted as what is not property in customary usage, such as a dirham or two dirhams, unless circumstantial evidence comes which would justify ruling for more than that.

The fifth form: that he says to him, "I have much property" or "great property." Al-Shafi'i said: It is accepted for a grain. The verse: ﴿Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it.﴾

In al-Tirmidhi: from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "When the Qur'an was revealed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he would move his tongue with it, wanting to memorize it. So Allah, blessed and exalted, revealed: ﴿Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it.﴾"

He said: "So he would move his lips with it." Sufyan moved his lips. Abu 'Isa (al-Tirmidhi) said: "This is a hadith that is ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ (good and sound)."

The wording in Muslim, from Ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, is: "The Prophet (ﷺ) would struggle with the revelation greatly, and he would move his lips. Ibn 'Abbas said to me: 'I will move them as the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to move them.' Sa'id said: 'I will move them as Ibn 'Abbas used to move them.' So he moved his lips, and Allah, mighty and majestic, revealed: ﴿Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it. Indeed, upon Us is its collection and its recitation.﴾"

He said: "Its collection in your breast, then you will recite it. So when We have recited it, follow its recitation."

He said: "Listen to it and be attentive. Then upon Us is its explanation." He said: "After that, whenever Jibril (peace be upon him) came to him, the Prophet (ﷺ) would listen. When Jibril (peace be upon him) departed, the Prophet (ﷺ) would recite it as he had been taught." Al-Bukhari also transmitted it.

A parallel to this verse is His saying: ﴿And do not hasten with the Qur'an before its revelation to you is completed.﴾ [Ta-Ha: 114], which has already been discussed [see vol. 11, p. 250].

Ash-Sha'bi said: "He would only hasten with its recitation when it was revealed to him, out of his love for it and the sweetness of it on his tongue. So he was forbidden from that until it was gathered, because some of it is connected to other parts." It was also said: "When revelation came down to him, peace be upon him, he would move his tongue along with the revelation, fearing that he would forget it. So there was revealed: ﴿And do not hasten with the Qur'an before its revelation to you is completed﴾ [Ta-Ha: 114], and there was revealed: ﴿We shall make you recite, so you will not forget﴾ [Al-A'la: 6], and there was revealed: ﴿Do not move your tongue with it.﴾"

Ibn 'Abbas said: "And its recitation" (وَقُرْآنَهُ), meaning: its being recited to you. According to al-Farra', "al-qira'ah" and "al-Qur'an" are both verbal nouns (maṣdar).

Qatadah said: "Follow its recitation" means: follow its laws and its rulings.

His saying: "Then upon Us is its explanation" means: the clarification of what it contains of the limits, the lawful and the unlawful. Qatadah said this. It was also said: it means the clarification of what it contains of promise and threat, and their verification. It was also said: it means that upon Us is to make it clear through your tongue.

It was also said: ﴿Nay﴾ means they do not pray nor give zakat, referring to the disbelievers of Makkah. ﴿Rather, you love﴾ means: rather, you love, O disbelievers of the people of Makkah, ﴿the hasty﴾, that is, the worldly abode and life in it, ﴿and leave behind﴾, that is, you abandon ﴿the Hereafter﴾ and working for it. In some tafsir it is reported: "The Hereafter is Paradise."

The people of Madinah and the Kufans recited ﴿tuḥibbūna﴾ and ﴿tadharūna﴾ with the letter ta' in both, in the second person. Whoever recited with ya' took it as a reference to His saying: ﴿The human will be informed﴾ [Al-Qiyamah: 13], and it has the sense of "people." Whoever recited with ta' took it as addressing them directly with rebuke, because that is more emphatic in purpose.
