His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Faces that day will be radiant, looking toward their Lord﴾. The first word, *nadira*, derives from *al-nadra*, which means beauty and blessing. The second derives from *al-nazar*, so the meaning is that the faces of the believers will be bright, beautiful and joyful. It is said: Allah made them radiant (*nadarahum Allah yanduruhum nadratan wa nadaratan*), and this means brightness, a comfortable life and wealth. From this root is the hadith: "May Allah make radiant the one who heard my saying and preserved it." ("Radiant" [*nadrah*] is narrated with both the light and the emphatic form. Originally it means beauty of face and brilliance.) *Ila rabbiha*: toward their Creator and Owner. *Nazirah*: they will look toward their Lord. This is the view of the majority of scholars. On this subject there is the hadith of Suhayb, transmitted by Muslim, which has already been discussed in *Yunus*, at His saying: ﴿For those who do good is the best reward and more﴾ (see vol. 8, p. 330). Ibn 'Umar used to say: "The most honoured of the people of Paradise before Allah are those who look at His Face morning and evening." Then he recited this verse: ﴿Faces that day will be radiant, looking toward their Lord.﴾ Yazid al-Nahwi narrated from 'Ikrimah, who said: "They will look toward their Lord with a [real] look." al-Hasan used to say: "Their faces were made radiant and they looked upon their Lord."

It has also been said that *al-nazar* here means waiting for the reward that they have with Allah. This is narrated from Ibn 'Umar and Mujahid. 'Ikrimah said: "They await the command of their Lord." al-Mawardi reported this from Ibn 'Umar and also from 'Ikrimah. However, it is only known from Mujahid alone. They argue with His saying: ﴿No vision can grasp Him, but He grasps all vision﴾ (al-An'am: 103). But this view is very weak and goes against the apparent meaning of the verse and the reports. In al-Tirmidhi, from Ibn 'Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The lowest of the people of Paradise in rank is the one who looks at his gardens, his wives, his servants and his couches for a distance of a thousand years, and the most honoured of them before Allah is the one who looks at His Face morning and evening." Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited: ﴿Faces that day will be radiant, looking toward their Lord.﴾ He said: "This is a strange (gharib) hadith. It has been narrated from Ibn 'Amr, but not traced to the Prophet ﷺ." In Sahih Muslim, from Abu Bakr ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Qays, from his father, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "There are two gardens of silver, their vessels and what is in them, and two gardens of gold, their vessels and what is in them. Nothing stands between the people and looking at their Lord, may He be Mighty and Majestic, except the cloak of His greatness over His Face in the Garden of Eden." Jarir ibn 'Abd Allah narrated: "We were sitting with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ when he looked at the moon on the night of the full moon and said: 'You will see your Lord plainly, just as you see this moon, and you will not be harmed in seeing Him. So if you can avoid being overcome in your prayer before sunrise and before sunset, then do so.'" Then he recited: ﴿And glorify your Lord with praise before the rising of the sun and before its setting﴾ (agreed upon by al-Bukhari and Muslim). Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi also transmitted it, and al-Tirmidhi said: "It is a good, sahih hadith." Abu Dawud transmitted from Abu Razin al-'Uqayli, who said: "I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, will all of us see our Lord?'" Ibn Mu'adh said: "[Seeing Him] alone (*mukhliyan bihi*) on the Day of Resurrection?" He said: "Yes, O Abu Razin." He said: "And what is the sign of that in His creation?" He said: "O Abu Razin, do not all of you see the moon?" Ibn Mu'adh said: "On the night of the full moon, [seeing it] alone." We said: "Yes." He said: "Then Allah is greater." [Ibn Mu'adh said: he said:] "It is only one of the creations of Allah, meaning the moon, and Allah is more Majestic and Greater." In the Kitab al-Nasa'i, from Suhayb, he said: "Then the veil will be lifted and they will look at Him. By Allah, Allah has given them nothing more beloved to them than looking [at Him], nor anything more pleasing to their eyes." In al-Tafsir of Abu Ishaq al-Tha'labi, from al-Zubayr, from Jabir, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Our Lord, may He be Mighty and Majestic, will manifest Himself until they look at His Face. Then they will fall down in prostration before Him. He will say: 'Raise your heads, for this is not a day of worship.'"

Al-Tha'labi said: The view of Mujahid that it means waiting for the reward from their Lord, and that no one among His creation sees Him, is a flawed interpretation, because when the Arabs intend by *al-nazar* waiting, they say *nazartuhu*, as Allah says: ﴿Do they await anything but the Hour?﴾ (al-Zukhruf: 66); ﴿Do they await anything but its fulfilment?﴾ (al-A'raf: 53); ﴿They await only a single blast﴾ (Ya-Sin: 49). When they intend reflection and contemplation, they say: *nazartu fihi* (I looked into it). But when *al-nazar* is connected with *ila* and with mention of the face, it can only mean seeing and direct sight.

Al-Azhari said: The saying of Mujahid, "they await the reward of their Lord," is an error, because one does not say *nazara ila kadha* to mean waiting. The saying of one who says "I looked at So-and-so" means only seeing with the eye, and this is how the Arabs speak. They say *nazartu ilayhi* when they mean looking with the eye, and when they mean waiting they say *nazartuhu*. The poet said:

"If you two look at me [wait for me] for a while
of time, it will benefit me with Umm Jundab."

When he meant waiting, he said *tanzurani* (you wait for me) and did not say *tanzurani ila*. When they mean looking with the eye, they say *nazartu ilayhi*. The poet said:

"I looked at her while the stars were like
lamps of monks kindled for the returning travellers."

(*Tashibb*: kindled. *Qaffal*: the plural of *qafil*, the one returning from a journey. This verse is from a qasida of Imru' al-Qays.)

Another said:

"I looked at her in al-Muhassab of Mina,
and I had a look, were it not for the restraint, that would harm [me]."

(In the manuscripts of the original it reads *nazrah*, but the correct reading is as we have mentioned, as it appears in the diwan of its composer, who is 'Umar ibn Rabi'ah.)

Another said:

"Indeed I am looking to you for what you promised us,
the look of the poor toward the wealthy rich man."

That is, I look at you in humility, because the look of humiliation and submission is more tender to the heart of the one being asked. As for what they used as evidence, His saying: ﴿No vision can grasp Him, but He grasps all vision﴾ (al-An'am: 103), this refers to the life of this world. This matter has already been discussed fully in its place (see vol. 7, p. 54).

'Atiyyah al-'Awfi said: "They look at Allah, and their sight does not encompass Him because of His greatness, but His sight encompasses them." This is indicated by: ﴿No vision can grasp Him, but He grasps all vision.﴾

Al-Qushayri Abu Nasr said: It has also been said that *ila* is the singular of *al-ala'* (the blessings), meaning: His blessings are awaited. This too is false, because the singular of *al-ala'* is written with an alif, not with a ya'. Then *al-ala'* means His blessings, the averting [of harm] (*al-duffa'*, as in all the manuscripts), and they in Paradise do not await the removal of His punishments from them. One who awaits something is a person whose life is troubled, and the people of Paradise are not described as such.

It has also been said: He attributed the look to the face, as in His saying: ﴿Rivers flow beneath them﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 119), where water flows in the river, not the river itself. Moreover, "face" is sometimes used to mean "eye." Allah says: ﴿Cast it upon the face of my father; he will regain his sight﴾ (Yusuf: 93), meaning upon his eyes. Furthermore, it is not far-fetched that on that Day the customary order will be reversed, so that Allah creates the sight and the looking in the face. This is like His saying: ﴿Is he who walks prone upon his face more rightly guided?﴾ (al-Mulk: 22). It was asked: "O Messenger of Allah, how will they walk in the Fire upon their faces?" He said: "He who made them walk upon their feet is able to make them walk upon their faces."

﴿And faces that day will be gloomy﴾: that is, the faces of the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection will be scowling, dark, frowning. In *al-Sihah*: *basara al-fahl al-naqah wa-ibtasaraha* means when the stallion mounted the she-camel without her being in heat. *Basara al-rajul wajhahu busuran* means he scowled, as it is said: he frowned and scowled. al-Suddi said: *basirah* means changed, and the meaning is the same.

﴿Expecting that some disaster will be inflicted upon them﴾: that is, they are certain and know. *Al-faqirah* is a calamity and a great matter. It is said: *faqarathu al-faqirah*, meaning the calamity broke his backbone. Mujahid and others said this. Qatadah said: *al-faqirah* is evil. al-Suddi: destruction. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Zayd: entering the Fire. The meanings are close. Its origin is branding the nose of a camel with an iron or fire until it reaches the bone. This was said by al-Asma'i. It is said: *faqartu anf al-ba'ir* means when you cut it with an iron, then placed a *jarir* (a halter of leather with which a camel is muzzled) on the place of the cut, and upon it a twisted cord, in order to tame and train it with that. From this is the saying: "He has treated him with the *faqirah*." al-Nabighah said:

"A grave that does not cease to face me has refused me,

He spoke of something that had not been mentioned before, because the addressee already knew it, as in His words: ﴿until it was hidden behind the veil﴾ [Sad 38:32], and His words: ﴿Why, then, when it reaches the throat﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 56:83]. This has already been discussed [see vol. 15, p. 195 and vol. 17, p. 230]. It has also been said that *kalla* means "truly," so the meaning is: truly, the driving toward God is when the collarbones are reached, that is, when the soul has ascended to the collarbones. Durayd ibn al-Simmah said [the text as it stands in the original; the verse belongs to his daughter Amrah, from a poem of hers lamenting her father, as in *Shu'ara' al-Nasraniyyah*]:

*"Many a great one you have defended them against,*
*when their souls had reached the collarbones."*

The reaching of the soul to the collarbones is sometimes used as a figure of speech for being on the brink of death. The purpose is to remind them of the severity of the situation at the arrival of death.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And it is said, "Who is a healer?"﴾

This has been disputed. It has been said that it is from *al-ruqyah* (incantation/healing), reported from Ibn Abbas, Ikrimah and others. Simak reported from Ikrimah that he said: *man raqin yarqi*, meaning: who will heal? Maymun ibn Mihran reported from Ibn Abbas: that is, is there a physician who can heal him? Abu Qilabah and Qatadah also said this, and the poet said:

*"Is there for the youth, of the vicissitudes of time, any protector,*
*or for him, from the sealed fate of death, any healer?"*

This was in the manner of astonishment and despair, meaning: who is able to heal from death? It is also reported from Ibn Abbas and Abu al-Jawza' that it is from *raqiya yarqa*, meaning: to ascend. The meaning then is: who will ascend with his spirit to heaven? Are they angels of mercy or angels of punishment? It has also been said that the Angel of Death says: "Who is the one who will ascend (with this soul)?", meaning: who will ascend with this soul? This is because the angels dislike the proximity of the soul of the disbeliever, so the Angel of Death says: "O so-and-so, go up with it."

Asim and a group [of reciters] made the nun clear in His words: ﴿man raq﴾ [i.e., they pronounced it with *idhhar*, clearly articulating the consonant]. The lam in His words *bal ran* [i.e., ﴿bal ran﴾ in 83:14] is [also pronounced clearly] lest it resemble *mariq*, which means a seller of broth, and *baran*, which is the dual of *al-barr* [the pious]. The correct practice is to omit the clear pronunciation; the kasrah on the qaf in *man raq* and the fathah on the nun in *bal ran* suffice to remove any ambiguity. A better approach than what has been mentioned is to intend a pause on *man* and *bal*, and to make them clear; this was said by al-Qushayri.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And he thought﴾, that is, the human being became certain ﴿that it was the parting﴾, that is, the parting from the world, family, wealth and children. This is at the moment he sees the angels. The poet said:

*"A parting unlike any other parting,*
*in which hope of meeting has been cut off."*

Qatadah said: Have you not seen him, when he is near death, striking one of his legs against the other? Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and al-Hasan also said: they are the two legs of the person when they are wrapped in the shroud. Zayd ibn Aslam said: the leg of the shroud is entwined with the leg of the dead person. Al-Hasan also said: his two legs die and his two shins become dry, so they cannot carry him, though they used to carry him about. Al-Nahhas said: the first opinion is the best of them. Ali ibn Abi Talhah reported from Ibn Abbas, regarding ﴿And the leg is entwined with the leg﴾: he said, "It is the last day of the world and the first day of the Hereafter, so severity meets severity, except for the one whom Allah has shown mercy." That is, the severity of the anguish of death meets the severity of the terror of the arrival. The evidence for this is His words: ﴿To your Lord, on that Day, is the driving﴾ [al-Qiyamah 75:30].

Mujahid said: "Affliction upon affliction," meaning: hardships followed one another upon him. Al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd said: two severe matters gathered upon him: people prepare his body, and the angels prepare his spirit. The Arabs only mention the leg in tribulations and great hardships, and from this comes their saying: "The world stood on a leg," and "The war stood on a leg." The poet said:

*"And war stood up with us on one leg."* [The first half of the line is: "Patience before us, for it is an evil that remains."]

This meaning has already passed at the end of surah *Nun wal-Qalam* [see vol. 18, p. 248]. Some said: the disbeliever's spirit is tormented at the departure of his soul; this is the first leg. In some tafsirs it is said: his angel who used to record his evil deeds will drive him. *Al-masaq* is the verbal noun of *saqa yasuqu*, like *al-maqal* from *qala yaqulu*.

[[Its first half: "And he had folded his side over a hidden (grudge)."]]

"Fa-awla thumma awla thumma awla ... wa-hal li-d-darr yuhlabu min maradd"

"Wa-awla an yakuna lahu al-wala'"

That is, it came close to being for him. He also recited:

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 75, verse 36–40:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Does man think that he will be left neglected?﴾ That is, does the son of Adam suppose that he will be left (yukhalla) unattended, neither commanded nor forbidden? This was said by Ibn Zayd and Mujahid, and from it comes the expression "camels left to graze (sudan)": grazing without a herdsman. It was also said: does he think he will be left in his grave in this state forever, never to be resurrected? And the poet said:

"So I swear by God, with the utmost oath... that God has created nothing left in vain (sudan)."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Was he not a drop of semen emitted (yumna)?﴾ That is, from a drop of water that is emitted (tumna) into the womb, that is, poured into it. It is for this reason that it is called (maniyy) because of the pouring out of blood. This has been mentioned earlier [see vol. 17, p. 118 and p. 216]. The nutfah is the little water; it is said: "nataf al-ma'" when it drips, that is, was he not a small quantity of water in the loins of the man and the breastbones of the woman? Hafs recited ﴿min maniyyin yumna﴾ with the ya', which is the recitation of Ibn Muhaysin, Mujahid, Ya'qub and Ayyash from Abu 'Amr, and Abu 'Ubayd preferred it because of the word maniy. The rest recited it with the ta' because of nutfah, and Abu Hatim preferred this.

(Then he was a clinging clot) That is, blood after the nutfah. That is, He arranged all of this to show the lowliness of his station. Then He said: (Then He fashioned) That is, He measured (fa-sawwa), that is, He formed him in proportion and balanced him, by placing the spirit in him. (Then He made of him) That is, of the human being. It was also said: of the maniy.

(two sexes, the male and the female) That is, the man and the woman. Those who hold that the hermaphrodite (khunthā) should be disregarded have argued from this. It has already passed in surah al-Shura [see vol. 16, p. 48] that this verse and its companion came out in the form of the majority, and it was discussed earlier at the beginning of surah al-Nisa' [see vol. 5, p. 3] as well, and we mentioned its ruling in the verse on inheritance, so there is no point in repeating it. (Is not that One able) That is, is not the One who was able to create this living soul (nasama) [in some copies: the fetus] from a drop of water, able (to give life to the dead)? That is, able to restore these bodies to their form for resurrection after decay. It is related from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that when he recited it he would say: [Glory be to You, O God, yes (bala)]. [Ibn Abbas said: whoever recites ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ [al-A'la: 1], whether he is an imam or otherwise, let him say: "Glory be to my Lord, the Most High," and whoever recites ﴿I swear by the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 1] to its end, whether he is an imam or otherwise, let him say: "Glory be to You, O God, yes."] Al-Tha'labi mentioned it from the hadith of Abu Ishaq al-Sabi'i from Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn Abbas. The surah is concluded, and praise is due to God.
